before: Running a red light is one of the most dangerous driving behaviors on the road. According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), red light running causes hundreds of deaths and tens of thousands of injuries every year in the United States. If a driver runs a red light and crashes into you, you would expect the fault question to be obvious — but the legal reality in Georgia and South Carolina is more nuanced than most people realize.
after: Running a red light is one of the most dangerous driving behaviors on the road. According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), red light running killed 1,119 people and injured more than 141,000 in 2024, and half of those killed were pedestrians, cyclists and people in other vehicles. If a driver runs a red light and crashes into you, you would expect the fault question to be obvious — but the legal reality in Georgia and South Carolina is more nuanced than most people realize.

before: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20, drivers facing a steady red signal must stop at the marked stop line or, if none, before entering the crosswalk or intersection. Running a red light is a traffic offense that carries fines and points on your license. In a civil case, the traffic violation serves as evidence of negligence per se — meaning the mere fact that the driver violated the statute can establish the duty and breach elements of a negligence claim, shifting the focus to causation and damages.
after: Under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-21, drivers facing a steady red signal must stop at the marked stop line or, if none, before entering the crosswalk or intersection. Running a red light is a misdemeanor under O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20 that carries fines and points on your license. In a civil case, the traffic violation serves as evidence of negligence per se — meaning the mere fact that the driver violated the statute can establish the duty and breach elements of a negligence claim, shifting the focus to causation and damages.

before:
Under S.C. Code § 56-5-970, drivers facing a steady red signal must stop before entering the crosswalk or intersection. As in Georgia, violating this statute constitutes evidence of negligence. South Carolina courts recognize the negligence per se doctrine, meaning a red light violation can establish that the driver breached their duty of care.

In both states, a traffic citation issued at the scene for running a red light is admissible evidence in a personal injury lawsuit and significantly strengthens your case.
after:
Under S.C. Code § 56-5-970, drivers facing a steady red signal must stop before entering the crosswalk or intersection. As in Georgia, violating this statute constitutes evidence of negligence. South Carolina courts recognize the negligence per se doctrine, meaning a red light violation can establish that the driver breached their duty of care.

In both states, however, the traffic citation itself is not admissible in the injury lawsuit (Georgia: Howard v. Lay; South Carolina: S.C. Code § 56-5-6160). If the other driver pleads guilty to running the red light, the jury may weigh that plea as an admission, though it is not conclusive (Gaddis v. Skelton; Samuel v. Mouzon), and the responding officer can testify to what they saw.

before: Red light cameras and traffic monitoring cameras can provide critical evidence in disputed-fault intersection crashes. However, their availability and legal status differ between Georgia and South Carolina.
after: Red light cameras can provide critical evidence in disputed-fault intersection crashes. However, their availability and legal status differ between Georgia and South Carolina.

before: Georgia law permits the use of automated traffic enforcement cameras in certain jurisdictions (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20(f)). Cities like Atlanta, Savannah, and others may operate red light camera programs. The photos and video captured by these cameras can be obtained through discovery and used as evidence in a personal injury case to prove the other driver entered the intersection after the light turned red.
after: Georgia law permits the use of automated traffic enforcement cameras in certain jurisdictions with a GDOT permit (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-20(f); O.C.G.A. § 40-14-21). As of GDOT's 2024 report, only Marietta, Savannah, Smyrna and Clayton County operate them, at twelve intersections statewide; Savannah's are all along Abercorn Street and DeRenne Avenue. If the crash happened at one of those intersections, the recorded images (the rear of the vehicle and its plate as it crosses on red) can be requested to show that the other driver's vehicle entered after the light turned red; by law the cameras do not capture the driver's identity (§ 40-14-21(j)).

before: South Carolina does not currently authorize red light cameras for automated traffic enforcement. However, many intersections have traffic monitoring cameras operated by the South Carolina Department of Transportation (SCDOT) for traffic management purposes. While these cameras are not designed to capture violations, the footage may still be available and useful as evidence. Additionally, surveillance cameras from nearby businesses, dashcams, and doorbell cameras near the intersection are increasingly valuable sources of video evidence.
after: South Carolina does not currently authorize red light cameras for automated traffic enforcement: a ticket for disregarding a traffic signal must be issued in person during a traffic stop and cannot be based on photographic evidence (S.C. Code § 56-7-35, enacted in 2011). The South Carolina Department of Transportation's traffic monitoring cameras stream live to 511SC but are not recorded, so no past footage exists to request. Instead, surveillance cameras from nearby businesses, dashcams, and doorbell cameras near the intersection are increasingly valuable sources of video evidence.

before: In cases involving particularly reckless behavior — such as a driver who ran a red light while intoxicated or while street racing — you may also recover punitive damages to punish the defendant. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1), with exceptions for DUI. South Carolina caps them at the greater of 3x compensatory damages or $500,000 (S.C. Code § 15-32-530).
after: In cases involving particularly reckless behavior — such as a driver who ran a red light while intoxicated or while street racing — you may also recover punitive damages to punish the defendant. Georgia caps punitive damages at $250,000 in most cases (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1(g)), with no cap where the defendant intended harm or drove while substantially impaired by alcohol or drugs (§ 51-12-5.1(f)). South Carolina caps them at the greater of 3x compensatory damages or $500,000, a floor indexed each year ($739,245 in 2026), with no cap for intended harm, a related felony plea or conviction, or substantial impairment by alcohol or drugs (S.C. Code § 15-32-530(C)).

before: Red light runners are not automatically liable for intersection crashes in Georgia or South Carolina. Fault is determined by examining whether the other driver was speeding, made an illegal turn, or failed to exercise caution entering the intersection. Both states apply modified comparative fault rules — Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more fault (O.C.G.A. SS 51-12-33), South Carolina at 51% or more. Red light camera footage, traffic signal timing data, and witness testimony help establish fault. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. SS 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code SS 15-3-530).
after: Red light runners are not automatically liable for intersection crashes in Georgia or South Carolina. Fault is determined by examining whether the other driver was speeding, made an illegal turn, or failed to exercise caution entering the intersection. Both states apply modified comparative fault rules — Georgia bars recovery at 50% or more fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), South Carolina at 51% or more (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Dashcam and surveillance video, traffic signal timing data, and witness testimony help establish fault; red light camera images exist only at Georgia's twelve permitted intersections and South Carolina has none. Filing deadlines are two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530).

before: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, a traffic citation issued at the scene is admissible evidence in a personal injury lawsuit. A citation for running a red light is strong evidence that the other driver breached their duty of care.
after: Not the ticket itself. In both states a traffic citation and any conviction on it are inadmissible in a civil case (Georgia: Howard v. Lay, 259 Ga. App. 391 (2003); South Carolina: S.C. Skelton, 226 Ga. App. 325 (1997); Samuel v. Mouzon, 282 S.C. 616 (Ct. App. 1984)). The responding officer can also testify to what they observed.
